name: CagriSema

lead: CagriSema is a once-weekly injection combining semaglutide with cagrilintide, an amylin analogue. People chasing large fat loss discuss it, sometimes alongside retatrutide, for the lower body fat and leaner look that comes with substantial weight loss.

Semaglutide activates GLP-1 receptors and cagrilintide activates amylin receptors; both reduce appetite through partly different pathways. A phase 3a trial in adults without diabetes found about 20% mean weight change over 68 weeks versus about 3% with placebo. It beat semaglutide alone in a meta-analysis of early trials, and in a developer-reported head-to-head trial it did not meet non-inferiority against tirzepatide.

paras: Novo Nordisk is developing it as a weekly injection for adults with overweight or obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes. It is used within clinical trials, and a new drug application was filed with the US FDA in December 2025.
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and constipation are the most reported effects, and were more frequent than with semaglutide alone. It has no approved label, and any supply outside trials is unregulated.

angle.text: CagriSema is a weekly cagrilintide and semaglutide shot used by people after large fat loss, sometimes compared with retatrutide. The two drugs cut appetite through different pathways, lowering body fat. Phase 3 trials showed about 20 percent weight loss in people with obesity; it is not approved.

lead: CagriSema is an investigational once-weekly injectable combination of cagrilintide, an amylin-receptor agonist, and semaglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, developed by Novo Nordisk for weight management and type 2 diabetes. [1][2][3] The appearance connection runs through fat loss: reduced appetite leads to lower body weight, which people pursue for a leaner body and face. It is not an appearance product in itself and is studied in adults with overweight or obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes. [1][4]

In the 68-week phase 3a REDEFINE 1 trial in adults without diabetes, the combination produced a mean body-weight change of about 20 percent versus about 3 percent with placebo, ahead of semaglutide alone (about 15 percent) and cagrilintide alone (about 12 percent), according to Wikipedia's summary of the trial. [4][3] A meta-analysis of three early randomized trials found greater weight loss than semaglutide 2.4 mg alone, with more gastrointestinal adverse events. [2] In an open-label head-to-head trial reported by the developer, it did not meet the non-inferiority endpoint against tirzepatide. [1]

Per Grokipedia, Novo Nordisk filed a new drug application with the US FDA in December 2025, and the product was not approved anywhere at the time of that source; a European filing and a 2027 launch were described as planned. [1] Online, CagriSema is mentioned alongside other newer peptides such as retatrutide, mostly as a coming successor to semaglutide. [5]
infobox: Amylin receptor agonist + GLP-1 receptor agonist (fixed combination)

paras: The studied use is chronic weight management in adults with obesity, or with overweight plus a weight-related condition, with or without type 2 diabetes [1][4][6]. Separate phase 3 programs have also examined its effects on blood glucose in type 2 diabetes and on blood pressure [7][8][9]. Registered trials include studies in adolescents with type 2 diabetes, people with hypertension and obesity, and weight-loss maintenance [10][11][12].

Developer-reported programmes beyond weight loss include REDEFINE 3, a cardiovascular outcomes trial that Grokipedia describes as ongoing, and a paediatric programme. [1] Cagrilintide alone has also been tested: Wikipedia reports a 2021 phase 2 dose-finding trial in The Lancet and, in REDEFINE 1, a mean 11.8 percent weight reduction with cagrilintide versus 2.3 percent with placebo. [13]

A phase 2 trial in type 2 diabetes tested the coadministration of cagrilintide 2.4 mg and semaglutide 2.4 mg against each agent alone [14]. In the 68-week phase 3a REDEFINE 1 trial in adults with overweight or obesity, CagriSema was compared with placebo and with each component alone [4]. Wikipedia lists results of -20.4% for CagriSema, -14.9% for semaglutide, -11.5% for cagrilintide and -3.0% for placebo among 3,417 participants, and Grokipedia reports about 80% of participants with gastrointestinal adverse events [3][1]. The companion trial in adults with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes (REDEFINE 2, 1,206 participants) reported smaller reductions: Wikipedia gives -13.7% versus -3.1% with placebo and Grokipedia gives 15.7% versus 3.1%, figures that appear to reflect different analysis conventions [6][3][1]. A blood-pressure analysis of REDEFINE 1 has also been published [8].

A 2024 meta-analysis of three randomized trials with 430 participants reported a mean difference of about -9 percentage points in weight versus semaglutide 2.4 mg at 20-32 weeks, with high heterogeneity; gastrointestinal events and vomiting were higher with the combination [2]. Phase 3 REIMAGINE trials in type 2 diabetes have been published in 2026 [7][9]. Recent network meta-analyses and reviews place CagriSema among next-generation obesity drugs expected to achieve weight loss in the range of tirzepatide [15][16][17][18][19].

In the REDEFINE 4 open-label head-to-head trial against tirzepatide 15 mg, as reported by Grokipedia, weight loss was 20.2% to 23.0% with CagriSema versus 23.6% to 25.5% with tirzepatide, and non-inferiority was not met [1]. Ongoing registered trials include a 2,500-person phase 3 study and a trial of switching from semaglutide [20][21].

A phase 2 programme preceded phase 3: Wikipedia reports average weight loss of 15.6 percent after 32 weeks in the earlier trial, with HbA1c improving more than with cagrilintide alone. [3] REDEFINE 5, a phase 3a trial in 331 participants in Japan and Taiwan, reported -18.4 percent with CagriSema versus -11.7 percent with semaglutide, according to Wikipedia. [3]

Network meta-analyses and reviews generally place CagriSema among next-generation obesity drugs, with weight loss expected near the range of tirzepatide. [15][16][19] A 2026 Guardian headline cited by Wikipedia described the drug as "obsolete" in the context of newer agents, though the article's content was not reviewed here. [3]

The reported adverse-event profile resembles that of the GLP-1 class: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and constipation, mostly mild to moderate [1][2]. Grokipedia reports about 6% discontinuation for adverse events and injection-site reactions in about 12% of users [1]. Since the product is unapproved, no official label or contraindication list exists.

The semaglutide component carries the class boxed warning on thyroid C-cell tumours seen in rodents and a contraindication in people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2, according to Wikipedia's semaglutide article; common effects of semaglutide are nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, constipation and abdominal pain, peaking during dose escalation, with gallstones and rare gastroparesis also reported. [22] Grokipedia lists acute pancreatitis and gallbladder disorders among serious risks noted for CagriSema. [1]

Semaglutide activates GLP-1 receptors and cagrilintide acts on amylin receptors; amylin is a hormone co-secreted with insulin that influences satiety and postprandial glucose [23][18]. Reviews describe combining hormones with complementary actions as a strategy to increase weight loss beyond GLP-1 agonism alone [16][17]. Grokipedia reports a 16-week dose-escalation period [1].
Wikipedia describes cagrilintide as a long-acting amylin analogue (also called GLXC-26801) and describes it elsewhere as a dual amylin and calcitonin receptor agonist. [13][3]

Because CagriSema is unapproved, any use outside trials would involve unregulated product. Posts in a T Nation thread group it with retatrutide and other research peptides that users describe positively. [5] Regulators have not authorised it for sale. [1]

The market context is semaglutide's commercial history. Wikipedia reports that Ozempic was approved by the FDA in December 2017 and Wegovy in June 2021, that shortages were declared from August 2022, that the Novo chief executive said up to 1.5 million Americans were using compounded GLP-1 products as of January 2026, and that counterfeit Ozempic pens were reported in Europe in October 2023. [22] Grokipedia says no price had been announced for CagriSema and cites one analyst estimate of up to $9.61 billion in US sales by 2037. [1]

lore.intro: CagriSema appears only briefly in community discussion, usually as an upcoming or research-grade successor to semaglutide, listed beside retatrutide. [5]

claims.claim: CagriSema "kicks ass" for fat loss alongside retatrutide
Adding an amylin analogue produces more fat loss than semaglutide alone.
CagriSema will match or surpass tirzepatide.
Weight loss from these drugs also costs muscle.
Research-peptide versions of new weight-loss drugs are interchangeable with the real product.

timeline.event: Semaglutide approved by the FDA as Ozempic for type 2 diabetes. [22]
Phase 2 dose-finding trial of once-weekly cagrilintide published in The Lancet; Wegovy approved for weight management. [13][22]
Phase 2 results of cagrilintide plus semaglutide in type 2 diabetes published in The Lancet; CagriSema enters phase 3. [14][3]
Meta-analysis of three randomized trials reports greater weight loss than semaglutide 2.4 mg alone. [2]
Phase 3a REDEFINE 1 and 2 results published in NEJM (June). [4][6][3]
Novo Nordisk reported to have filed an FDA application (December). [1]
REIMAGINE type 2 diabetes trials and REDEFINE 5 (Japan, Taiwan) published. [7][9][3]
